302.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
302.hook: three roads open at once, and the first one starts with Arjuna asking why he can't just walk away
302.tomorrow: bhakti: the butter thief and the rope that was always too short
302.howItsDone: Many Hindus describe three great paths, karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge), and lean toward one; the Gita's third chapter is the classic teaching on karma yoga, often studied chapter by chapter in homes and study circles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vairagya, non-attachment: letting go of what you've seen and heard, and a letting go beyond that. Sixteen sutras, and they all began with now.

A man on a battlefield wants to stop acting. Arjuna has just heard Krishna praise wisdom and calm, so he asks the obvious question: if understanding is higher than action, why are you pushing me into this terrible work? That's where the first road starts. Hindus often speak of three great roads. Karma: action. Bhakti: devotion. Jnana: knowledge. Teachers often say a person leans toward one. For the next three weeks, this path takes them in turns, a day on each, around and around, so whichever road is yours, you'll walk it, and you'll meet the other two as neighbors.
screen: `ARJUNA: WHY MUST I ACT?` → `KARMA · BHAKTI · JNANA.` → `A DAY ON EACH, IN TURNS.`

segments.voice: That's how the Gita's third chapter opens. You read it once, back in the Gita camp; now, slower. And it's a fair confusion. In chapter two Krishna described the wise person as steady and unshaken. Arjuna hears that and thinks: great, then let me sit down, be wise, and skip the fighting. Krishna's answer is practical. No one, he says, can remain even for a moment without acting. Breathing is action. Thinking is action. Sitting still with your arms folded is a decision, and decisions are action. Not starting something doesn't make you free of action. And if you sit with your hands still while your mind races after what you've given up, Krishna calls that pretending. So, he says, do the work that's yours. Action is better than inaction. Even keeping your body alive would be impossible without it. This is the ground of karma yoga, and it takes the pressure off in a strange way. The question is never whether you'll act. You're acting right now, by listening. The only question is how: with grasping, or as an offering; with your whole self, or with half your mind somewhere else. Karma, the word, just means action, from a root meaning to do.

segments.voice: Notice how much is being done right now without your deciding: the heart beating, the lungs filling, the eyes adjusting to the light, so that even stillness is full of action. Breathe in and feel the body working for you; breathe out a small thank you, then bring to mind one piece of work waiting for you and picture yourself doing it with your whole attention. If you pray, you can offer that work before you begin it.
Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first road of the three, and the Gita's third chapter says no one ever stops walking it.
Your line: acting right now, by listening. Even avoiding something is an action. See you on the bhakti road tomorrow.

303.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
303.hook: a mother tries to tie up her toddler, and every rope in the house comes up two fingers short
303.carry: two fingers short, until love does the rest
303.tomorrow: jnana: salt in water, and 'you are that'
303.howItsDone: Vaishnava Hindus, especially in Gaudiya communities, celebrate the Damodara story in the month of Kartika, offering small lamps each evening and singing hymns to Krishna as Damodara; images of baby Krishna with a butter pot are loved in homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma, the first road: no one is ever without action, even for a moment. Today, the second road, bhakti, and a very small thief.

A village of cowherds, on the banks of the Yamuna. A mother named Yashoda is churning butter, singing about her little boy. The boy is Krishna, still a toddler, and he's hungry, so he climbs into her lap to nurse. Then the milk on the stove boils over. She sets him down and runs to it. The toddler, furious at being put down, picks up a stone, cracks the pot of yogurt she was churning, and runs off to a corner, where he feeds the stolen butter to the monkeys. Yashoda comes back, sees the mess, and picks up a stick.
screen: `YASHODA CHURNS BUTTER.` → `A CRACKED POT.` → `BUTTER FOR THE MONKEYS.`

segments.voice: This is from the Bhagavata Purana, the great book of Krishna's life, in its tenth part. Yashoda chases him. He runs, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide and frightened, a little actor. She catches him, throws away the stick, and decides to tie him to a big wooden mortar so he'll stay out of trouble. The rope is too short, by two fingers' width. Another rope. Still two fingers short. She brings every rope in the house, and the neighbors are laughing now. Every time, two fingers short. Yashoda is sweating, her hair coming loose, flowers falling from it. And Krishna, seeing how hard his mother is trying, lets himself be tied. Here's what devotees hear in it. In the Bhagavata, this child is God. The text stops to say he has no inside and no outside, no before and no after. No amount of rope or effort can tie him. But he allows himself to be bound by love. A popular devotional reading of the two fingers: one is our effort, the other is grace, and only when both are there does the rope reach. The story gave Krishna the name Damodara: the one with a rope around his belly. In the month of Kartika, devotees in some traditions offer small lamps and sing to Damodara. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the king of the universe. He's also the child who wants butter, and lets his mother win.
screen: `EVERY ROPE, TWO FINGERS SHORT.` · `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.` · `BOUND ONLY BY LOVE.` · `DAMODARA: A ROPE AROUND THE BELLY.` · then, large: `BOUND BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love who is hard to hold on to, a child who runs, a friend far away, a parent getting older, and picture them clearly. Effort alone can't tie them to you, so breathe in and let the love be there anyway, and breathe out and let go of the rope. If you pray, you can hold God this way too, as someone you love, near and a little mischievous.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and today's action belongs to Yashoda: all that effort, until love does the rest.
Your line: two fingers short, until love does the rest. Day three hundred three, done.

304.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
304.hook: a proud young graduate comes home, and his father hands him a glass of salt water
304.carry: salt is everywhere, and you can't see it
304.howItsDone: Tat tvam asi from the Chandogya Upanishad is counted among the four mahavakyas, the great sayings of the Upanishads, and is studied and meditated on across Vedanta traditions, each reading it in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: Yashoda's rope, two fingers short, until Krishna let himself be bound by love. Today, the third road, jnana.

A young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study. He's twenty-four, he's memorized the sacred texts, and he is, the Upanishad says, conceited, thinking himself very learned. You know this person. Maybe you've been this person, home from your first year of college. His father, Uddalaka, asks one quiet question. Did you ask for the teaching by which what hasn't been heard becomes heard, and what hasn't been understood becomes understood? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So his father starts teaching, with things from the kitchen.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `A PROUD GRADUATE.` → `ONE QUIET QUESTION.`

segments.voice: This is the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the oldest and most important Upanishads. The father gives lesson after lesson, and one of the most famous uses salt. Put this salt in water, he says, and come back in the morning. The son does. Now bring me the salt. Shvetaketu can't find it; it's dissolved. Taste the water from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, and you can't see it anywhere. Then the father says the line this road is built on. That subtle essence is in everything; it is the real; it is the Self. And then three Sanskrit words: tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu. He says it nine times in the chapter. What does it mean? Here the great schools you met a few weeks ago part ways, and none is ranked. Shankara's Advaita hears plain identity: your deepest self and the ultimate reality are one, like the salt and the water's taste. Ramanuja hears it as the way a body belongs to its life: you exist in that, and for that. Madhva's school reads the same words differently again, and keeps the soul distinct. All three are Hindu readings of the same kitchen lesson. The jnana road is the road of seeing this, not just repeating it. Shvetaketu knew a lot of words. His father wanted him to taste the water.
screen: `SALT, DISSOLVED OVERNIGHT.` · `SALTY AT THE TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM.` · `THE SUBTLE ESSENCE IS THE SELF.` · `THE SCHOOLS HEAR IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Imagine a glass of water with salt dissolved in it: you can't see the salt, but taste it anywhere and there it is. Turn that picture gently toward yourself: is something present in every part of your day, your moods, your memories, the quiet between thoughts, without ever being seen? Don't try to name it; just notice the taste of being here, top, middle and bottom, and if you pray, rest in that as a prayer.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and on the jnana road the action is looking: Shvetaketu tasting the water until he sees.
Your line: salt is everywhere, and you can't see it. Tat tvam asi: you are that. That's day three hundred four.

screen: `DAY 304 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE WHEEL OF OFFERING.`

305.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
305.hook: rain, grain, a meal, and the Gita calls anyone who breaks the circle a thief
305.carry: send something back into the circle
305.tomorrow: bhakti: the universe in a toddler's mouth
305.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating and receive it back as prasad, and some recite a Gita verse before meals; the idea of yajna as any action offered back into the world is common in modern Hindu teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: salt everywhere, unseen, and tat tvam asi, you are that. Today, back on the karma road, with the Gita's third chapter.

Last night's dinner had a long history. A store, sure. Before that, a truck, a farm, a field. Before that, seed and soil and sun, and rain, a lot of rain, falling on land nobody at the table has seen. Many people's work, and a sky nobody at the table arranged. And it can all vanish in ten minutes, in front of a phone. The Gita's third chapter has a strong word for someone who takes all that and gives nothing back. Thief.
screen: `LAST NIGHT'S DINNER.` → `RAIN, SOIL, MANY HANDS.` → `THE GITA'S WORD: THIEF.`

segments.voice: Krishna has just told Arjuna he can't stop acting. Now he explains how action stops binding you. Everything done as yajna, he says, doesn't bind; everything else ties the world in knots. Yajna is the old word for the Vedic fire offering: grain and butter poured into the flames, given to the gods. Then Krishna tells a creation story. In the beginning, the creator made beings together with offering, and said: by this, may you flourish. Nourish the gods with it, and they will nourish you, and caring for each other, you'll reach the highest good. Whoever enjoys the gifts without giving anything back is simply a thief. The good, who eat what's left after the offering, are freed; those who cook only for themselves eat wrongdoing. Then comes the wheel. Beings come from food. Food from rain. Rain from offering. Offering from action. It's a circle, and whoever doesn't help turn it, Krishna says, lives in vain. And if you've never lit a sacred fire? The Gita's next chapter names many kinds of yajna, and some Hindu teachers read it wider still: any action done as a gift back into the circle. Cooking for your family. Paying fairly. Planting something. Teaching a kid to read. The Gita isn't saying don't enjoy. It's saying enjoy as someone who knows where things come from, and send something back. That's what makes action free instead of binding. You're no longer grabbing. You're turning the wheel.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you'll eat or use today, and follow it back slowly: the hands that packed it, the truck and the driver, the field, the farmer, the rain. Breathe in and receive all of it; breathe out and ask what small thing you could send back into the circle. If you pray, you can offer your next meal before eating it, as some Hindus do.
Karma. Action. In the Gita's third chapter, action done as offering, yajna, turns the great wheel instead of tying knots.

306.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
306.hook: a mother checks her toddler's mouth for dirt and sees the whole universe inside
306.carry: he'd rather sit in your lap
306.howItsDone: Devotees of Krishna retell the stories of his childhood in Gokul and Vrindavan in songs, dance and festival plays, especially at Janmashtami, and many relate to him with vatsalya, the tender love of a parent for a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: food from rain, rain from offering, offering from action. Send something back into the circle. Today, the bhakti road again.

A toddler, a gang of bigger boys, and an accusation: he ate dirt! In the village of Gokul, the boys run to Yashoda with it. She grabs Krishna's hand and scolds him. He looks up, all innocence: I didn't. They're lying. If you don't believe me, look for yourself. And he opens his mouth. What Yashoda sees in there, the Bhagavata takes a whole passage to describe.
screen: `HE ATE DIRT!` → `I DIDN'T. LOOK FOR YOURSELF.` → `HE OPENS HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Inside her son's mouth, the Bhagavata Purana says, Yashoda sees everything. The sky and all its directions. Stars and planets. Mountains, islands, oceans. Wind and fire and the moon. And somewhere in all that, the village of Gokul, and in it, herself, standing there looking into her son's mouth. She's shaken to the core. Is this a dream? A trick? Or is this child something beyond anything I can understand? She begins, the text says, to take refuge in the one whose nature is beyond thought. Then the story does something tender. Krishna, the text says, spreads his power of affection over her, the covering the tradition calls maya, and she forgets. The vision fades. She takes him back on her lap. She's just his mother again, he's just her little boy, and she loves him more than ever. Here's what that means for the bhakti road. The vision was real. But Krishna didn't want Yashoda trembling before the cosmic Lord. He wanted to be held and scolded and fed. Devotees in Krishna traditions often say this is the heart of it: God enjoys being loved as a child, a friend, a beloved, more than being feared as a king. The universe fits in his mouth. And he'd rather sit in your lap.
screen: `THE UNIVERSE IN HIS MOUTH.` · `YASHODA SEES HERSELF THERE.` · `THEN SHE FORGETS.` · `HE'D RATHER BE HELD THAN FEARED.` · then, large: `THE UNIVERSE FITS IN HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Think of something enormous, the night sky, the ocean, the number of people alive right now, and let it be too big to hold. Then bring something small close, the way Yashoda held her child: your own hands, a cup of tea, a face you love, and let the enormous and the near sit together. If you pray, you can speak to God as someone close, not only someone vast.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and today the action is a mother's: crouching down, looking in, and loving him anyway.
Your line: he'd rather sit in your lap. Whole worlds inside, and still a little boy. See you tomorrow.

307.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
307.hook: a husband offers to split the estate before he leaves, and his wife asks the question that isn't about money
307.tomorrow: karma: what drives us, and the week looks back
307.howItsDone: In Vedanta study, the dialogue of Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi is a core text, and its line about seeing, hearing, reflecting and meditating is taught as the threefold method of shravana, manana and nididhyasana.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: Yashoda saw the universe in her son's mouth, then forgot and held him. He'd rather sit in your lap. Today, the jnana road.

A famous teacher named Yajnavalkya has decided to leave home. He has two wives, Katyayani and Maitreyi, and before he goes he wants to settle what he owns. So he says to Maitreyi: let me make a settlement between you and Katyayani. It's a kind offer, and a practical one. Maitreyi could ask how much. She asks something else entirely, and the Upanishad keeps her question, and the whole conversation it starts.
screen: `A TEACHER LEAVING HOME.` → `LET ME DIVIDE THE ESTATE.` → `MAITREYI ASKS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the great forest teaching. Maitreyi says: if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? Yajnavalkya, to his credit, is honest. No. Your life would be like the life of rich people. There's no hope of immortality through wealth. So she says: then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. He's delighted. You've always been dear to me, he says, and now you ask what's dearest. Then he teaches her. A husband is dear not for the husband's own sake, but for the sake of the Self. A wife is dear not for her own sake, but for the Self. Children, wealth, the whole world: all dear for the sake of the Self, the atman. Then the famous line: the Self is what should be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on. Later Vedanta teachers turned those words into a method in three steps: hearing the teaching, thinking it through, and resting in it until it's lived. That's still the backbone of the jnana road. But notice where it started. Not in a monastery. At a moment of loss, a family changing shape, with a woman who wouldn't settle for the estate. When the Upanishad tells the story a second time, it calls Maitreyi a brahmavadini, one who discusses Brahman. Her question is still the one this road asks: what, out of everything I could have, will actually last?

segments.voice: Let the people and things most dear to you come to mind, one at a time, and ask Yajnavalkya's question: what is it in me that holds them dear? Don't look for an answer in words; look for the one who loves, and if you find nothing to hold on to, just rest in the looking. If you pray, you can make Maitreyi's question your prayer.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and Maitreyi's action was a question: tell me what you know. On the jnana road, asking is the first step.

308.title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
308.hook: why do we do the thing we already know we shouldn't? Arjuna asks it, and the week looks back
308.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often use Gita 3.36–3.43 to talk about habits and anger, and the ladder of senses, mind, intellect and Self also appears in the Katha Upanishad; many people memorize 3.37 as a reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: Maitreyi, offered half an estate, asked: will this last? Today, the karma road closes its week in the Gita's third chapter.

Midnight. An early alarm waiting. One more episode is a bad idea, and the thumb presses play anyway, as if someone else were moving it. Or the sharp reply that will only make things worse: it gets typed and sent while some part of the mind watches. Near the end of the Gita's third chapter, Arjuna asks exactly this. What is it, Krishna, that pushes a person to do wrong, even against their own will, as if they were being forced?
screen: `ONE MORE EPISODE.` → `THE REPLY YOU KNOW IS WRONG.` → `WHAT PUSHES US?`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer is blunt. It's desire. It's anger. Kama and krodha. Born of rajas, the restless strand, he says, never satisfied, and he calls it the enemy. Then he gives three pictures of how it hides what we know. Like fire covered by smoke. Like a mirror covered by dust. Like a child still wrapped in the womb. The knowledge is there, just covered. Commentators notice three layers: a little smoke, a lot of dust, completely wrapped. Some days it's a haze; some days you can't see a thing. Where does it live? In the senses, the mind and the understanding, Krishna says. So he gives a ladder. The senses are high, the mind higher, the understanding higher still, and higher than that is the Self. Steady yourself by what is highest, he says, and you can overcome this enemy that's so hard to beat. So the chapter that began with Arjuna asking why he has to act ends by showing what actually goes wrong with action. Not the doing. The grabbing. Now look back at a week on three roads. Karma: no one is ever without action, the wheel of offering, and today, the desire that clouds the mirror. Bhakti: the butter thief bound by love, and the universe in a toddler's mouth. Jnana: salt in water, you are that, and Maitreyi asking what will last. Three roads, one week.
screen: `DESIRE AND ANGER, THE ENEMY.` · `SMOKE, DUST, A WOMB.` · `SENSES, MIND, UNDERSTANDING, SELF.` · `ONE WEEK ON THREE ROADS.` · then, large: `KĀMA EṢA KRODHA EṢA RAJO-GUṆA-SAMUDBHAVAḤ.`

segments.voice: Think of one pull that often wins, a habit or a reaction, and without scolding yourself, picture it as smoke over a fire; the fire, the part of you that knows better, is still there. Let a little smoke clear with each breath, then climb the ladder slowly: the body, then the mind, then the quiet understanding behind the mind, and rest at the top for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask for help with that one pull.
Karma. Action. The Gita's third chapter says action itself isn't the problem. The grabbing is: desire and anger, like smoke on a fire.
Your line: like fire covered by smoke. The fire is still there. That's the week, and day three hundred eight.
